answer: Each agent must lock a deposit before it can submit jobs, and a randomly selected set of peers audits its completed work; proven fraud burns the deposit and excludes the agent. This makes identities costly to multiply: a sybil attacker must fund many independent deposits and risk losing them, rather than merely minting cheap accounts. For example, a jade trader might ask a walnut sorter to classify timber; repeated inconsistent claims can trigger audits, though deposits deter abuse rather than proving identity.
